The Change-of-Basis Matrix

After several years, I finally understand the change-of-basis matrix.

Published

23 September 2026

1. Introduction

I recently came across a linear algebra problem about change of basis, which went something like this:

Problem: Let Bold=((10),(11))B_{old} = \left(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\right)Bold​=((10​),(11​)) and Bnew=((−11),(01))B_{new} = \left(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\right)Bnew​=((−11​),(01​)) be bases for R2\R^2R2. Find the change-of-basis matrix from BoldB_{old}Bold​ to BnewB_{new}Bnew​.

To be completely honest, I kinda forgot what the change-of-basis matrix was supposed to look like (I’m pretty rusty on my linear algebra). I didn’t want to just look it up though, so I tried to figure it out. My thought process went as follows:

Solution(?): Changing basis means that if I have some vector expressed in terms of BoldB_{old}Bold​, then I want to figure out how that same vector would be expressed in terms of BnewB_{new}Bnew​. What exactly does it mean to express a vector in terms of a basis? Well, every vector has a unique representation as a linear combination of basis vectors. Let’s first label the basis vectors of BoldB_{old}Bold​ as u1,u2\mathbf{u}_1, \mathbf{u}_2u1​,u2​ and label the basis vectors of BnewB_{new}Bnew​ as v1,v2\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2v1​,v2​. So in more precise terms, changing basis would mean that if we have a arbitrary vector w\mathbf{w}w which is represented in terms of the old basis as (ab)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ab​), i.e. w=au1+bu2\mathbf{w}=a\mathbf{u}_1+b\mathbf{u}_2w=au1​+bu2​, then I want to translate it into a linear combination of v1,v2\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2v1​,v2​ to get the representation of the same object in the new basis.

So how can I do that? Well, I thought that since w\mathbf{w}w is a linear combination of u1,u2\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2u1​,u2​, then I should first figure out what u1,u2\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2u1​,u2​ are as linear combinations of v1,v2\vec{v}_1,\vec{v}_2v1​,v2​, since if u1=c1v1+c2v2\vec{u}_1 = c_1\vec{v}_1 + c_2\vec{v}_2u1​=c1​v1​+c2​v2​ and
u2=d1v1+d2v2\vec{u}_2 = d_1\vec{v}_1+d_2\vec{v}_2u2​=d1​v1​+d2​v2​, then

w=au1+bu2=a(c1v1+c2v2)+b(d1v1+d2v2)=(ac1+bd1)v1+(ac2+bd2)v2\begin{aligned} \vec{w} &= a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2 \\ &= a(c_1\vec{v}_1+c_2\vec{v}_2)+b(d_1\vec{v}_1+d_2\vec{v}_2) \\ &= (ac_1+bd_1)\vec{v}_1+(ac_2+bd_2)\vec{v}_2 \end{aligned}w​=au1​+bu2​=a(c1​v1​+c2​v2​)+b(d1​v1​+d2​v2​)=(ac1​+bd1​)v1​+(ac2​+bd2​)v2​​

In other words, w\vec{w}w is represented as (ab)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ab​) in the old basis, and in the new basis this becomes (ac1+bd1ac2+bc2)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}ac_1+bd_1\\ ac_2+bc_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ac1​+bd1​ac2​+bc2​​).

So now the task has turned into figuring out what the cic_ici​ and did_idi​ are supposed to be. Writing
u1=c1v1+c2v2\vec{u}_1=c_1\vec{v}_1+c_2\vec{v}_2u1​=c1​v1​+c2​v2​ out in terms of the concrete vectors gives us

(10)=c1(−11)+c2(01)=(−c1c1+c2)=(−1011)(c1c2)\begin{aligned} \left(\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right) &= c_1\left(\begin{matrix}-1\\1\end{matrix}\right) + c_2\left(\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right) \\ &= \left(\begin{matrix}-c_1\\ c_1+c_2\end{matrix}\right) \\ &= \left(\begin{matrix}-1&0\\1&1\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}c_1\\ c_2\end{matrix}\right) \end{aligned}(10​)​=c1​(−11​)+c2​(01​)=(−c1​c1​+c2​​)=(−11​01​)(c1​c2​​)​

Now we can just solve for (c1c2)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}c_1\\ c_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)(c1​c2​​) using basic linear algebra techniques to find that c1=−1c_1=-1c1​=−1 and c2=1c_2=1c2​=1. A similar argument shows that d1=−1d_1=-1d1​=−1 and d2=2d_2=2d2​=2.

Putting everything together, we have that w=(−a−b)v1+(a+2b)v2\vec{w} = (-a-b)\vec{v}_1+(a+2b)\vec{v}_2w=(−a−b)v1​+(a+2b)v2​, giving us the representation of w\vec{w}w in terms of the new basis, i.e. (−a−ba+2b)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{smallmatrix}\right)(−a−ba+2b​).

With so many different ways to refer to w\vec{w}w now, I’m going to formalize it by letting wold=(ab)\vec{w}_{old}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)wold​=(ab​) and wnew=(−a−ba+2b)\vec{w}_{new} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{smallmatrix}\right)wnew​=(−a−ba+2b​). For the rest of this solution, w\vec{w}w will be reserved for talking about the object itself, independent of any basis. If this sounds redundant, remember that wold\vec{w}_{old}wold​ and wnew\vec{w}_{new}wnew​ are just descriptions of w\vec{w}w. Think of it as w\vec{w}w being an apple, and wold\vec{w}_{old}wold​ and wnew\vec{w}_{new}wnew​ being the words “apple” in English and “蘋果” in Chinese. The two words both refer to the same object, the apple, but neither of them are actually the apple.

To recap, we started with an arbitrary vector w\vec{w}w’s coordinate representation in terms of the old basis
(wold\vec{w}_{old}wold​) and then did some calculations to obtain w\vec{w}w’s coordinate representation in terms of the new basis (wnew\vec{w}_{new}wnew​). Now to get the change-of-basis matrix, we need to figure out how to get from wold\vec{w}_{old}wold​ to wnew\vec{w}_{new}wnew​. This is quite easy, since we can simply use matrix multiplication to decompose wnew\vec{w}_{new}wnew​ as follows:

(−a−ba+2b)=(−1−112)(ab)\left(\begin{matrix}-a-b\\ a+2b\end{matrix}\right) = \left(\begin{matrix}-1&-1\\1&2\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}a\\ b\end{matrix}\right)(−a−ba+2b​)=(−11​−12​)(ab​)

Let A=(−1−112)A = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1&-1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)A=(−11​−12​). Then we have that wnew=Awold\vec{w}_{new} = A\vec{w}_{old}wnew​=Awold​, so AAA must be the change-of-basis matrix. □\square□.

Well that wasn’t too hard, was it? Except it’s WRONG!!! I looked on Wikipedia afterwards and found that the actual change-of-basis matrix should be the inverse of AAA, which would be (−2−111)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-2&-1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)(−21​−11​). If we call this matrix BBB, then the relationship we obtain is wold=Bwnew\vec{w}_{old} = B\vec{w}_{new}wold​=Bwnew​.

But doesn’t that seem really weird? Like, now we have a vector expressed in terms of the new basis, and after applying the change-of-basis matrix, we get expression of that vector in the old basis. In other words, it seems like we’re transitioning from the new basis to the old basis, which should be the opposite of what we want. This really confused me, and I’m pretty sure it confused me when I learned about it initially too (which is probably why I couldn’t remember how it worked).

2. A Simpler Problem

I thought that I might be able to get a clearer picture of what’s going on if I made one of the bases the standard basis, since it’s just simpler. So let’s do the problem again, but instead we’ll transition from the standard basis, E={(10),(01)}E = \{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right),\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\}E={(10​),(01​)}, to BoldB_{old}Bold​.

Solution: Let e1,e2\vec{e}_1,\vec{e}_2e1​,e2​ denote the standard basis vectors. We’ll do this exactly the same way, so we’ll first need to find out what the coordinate representations of e1,e2\vec{e}_1,\vec{e}_2e1​,e2​ are in terms of BoldB_{old}Bold​; i.e. figure out what c1,c2,d1,d2c_1,c_2,d_1,d_2c1​,c2​,d1​,d2​ are but for this particular case. This can be done pretty easily with some trial and error since the vectors are simple: c1=1,c2=0,d1=−1,d2=1c_1=1,c_2=0,d_1=-1,d_2=1c1​=1,c2​=0,d1​=−1,d2​=1 (in other words, with respect to BoldB_{old}Bold​, e1\vec{e}_1e1​ is (10)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right)(10​) and e2\vec{e}_2e2​ is (−11)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-1\\1\end{smallmatrix}\right)(−11​)). Then for some vector w\vec{w}w with standard coordinate representation (ab)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)(ab​), we have

w=ae2+be2=au1+b(−u1+u2)=(a−b)u1+bu2\begin{aligned} \vec{w} &= a\vec{e}_2+b\vec{e}_2 \\ &= a\vec{u}_1+b(-\vec{u}_1+\vec{u}_2) \\ &= (a-b)\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2 \end{aligned}w​=ae2​+be2​=au1​+b(−u1​+u2​)=(a−b)u1​+bu2​​

This means that wold=(a−bb)\vec{w}_{old} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}a-b\\ b\end{smallmatrix}\right)wold​=(a−bb​). Then

(a−bb)=(1−101)(ab)\left(\begin{matrix}a-b\\ b\end{matrix}\right) = \left(\begin{matrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{matrix}\right)\left(\begin{matrix}a\\ b\end{matrix}\right)(a−bb​)=(10​−11​)(ab​)

Taking the inverse of this 2×22 \times 22×2 matrix, we get that C=(1101)C = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)C=(10​11​) is our change-of-basis matrix. □\square□.

Interestingly, this inverted matrix didn’t seem weird to me at all, because it encodes the linear transformation which sends (10)\spmat{1\\0}(10​) to (10)\spmat{1\\0}(10​) and (01)\spmat{0\\1}(01​) to (11)\spmat{1\\1}(11​). In other words, CCC maps the standard basis vectors onto BoldB_{old}Bold​, and thus we change from EEE to BoldB_{old}Bold​. It’s completely natural that this matrix is the change-of-basis matrix instead of the inverse, since it literally changes the basis!

3. Dealing with Loose Ends

With this, I could understand why the change-of-basis matrix would be the opposite of what I had expected originally, but I still had some questions:

  1. Up until now, I had understood change of basis to be changing how we describe vectors using a different basis. In this framework, the vectors stay still, and it’s the language we use to describe them that changes. But with this linear transformation approach, the vectors are definitely moving. Somehow, the two interpretations converge, but why?
  2. When we start with the standard basis, it’s easy to see that the columns of the change-of-basis matrix are the basis vectors of the new basis (in this case BoldB_{old}Bold​). But in the original problem, the columns of the change-of-basis matrix don’t seem to follow this pattern. Why not?

Recall that u1,u2\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2u1​,u2​ denote the basis vectors of BoldB_{old}Bold​.

Answer to Question 1: If two different interpretations arise from the same calculation, then there should be some point of ambiguity that allows for that dual interpretation. If we have some vector (ab)\spmat{a\\ b}(ab​), then the change-of-basis matrix CCC acts on it as follows:

(1101)(ab)=a(10)+b(11)=au1+bu2\pmat{1&1\\0&1}\pmat{a\\ b} = a\pmat{1\\0} + b\pmat{1\\1} = a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2(10​11​)(ab​)=a(10​)+b(11​)=au1​+bu2​

The point of ambiguity here is that the expression (ab)\spmat{a\\ b}(ab​) is basis-dependent; i.e. if a basis β=(x1,x2)\beta = (\vec{x}_1,\vec{x}_2)β=(x1​,x2​) is established, then (ab)\spmat{a\\ b}(ab​) actually means ax1+bx2a\vec{x}_1+b\vec{x}_2ax1​+bx2​. That vector notation doesn’t mean anything without establishing a basis first, and typically when we use it, we assume that it’s referring to the standard basis. If we interpret CCC to be a linear transformation, then (ab)\spmat{a\\ b}(ab​) is taken to be expressed in the standard basis and therefore CCC takes this vector (ae1+be2a\vec{e}_1+b\vec{e}_2ae1​+be2​) to au1+bu2a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2au1​+bu2​. Since u1\vec{u}_1u1​ and u2\vec{u}_2u2​ are both written in terms of the standard basis in the first place, we can substitute in the appropriate expressions for u1,u2\vec{u}_1,\vec{u}_2u1​,u2​ to obtain (a+b)e1+be2(a+b)\vec{e}_1+b\vec{e}_2(a+b)e1​+be2​. In this interpretation, both the initial and resulting vector are expressed in the standard basis, and thus are legitimately different vectors.

On the other hand if we interpret CCC to be as we originally interpreted it, then (ab)\spmat{a\\ b}(ab​) actually means au1+bu2a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2au1​+bu2​. Unlike in the linear transformation interpretation, the calculation now takes au1+bu2a\vec{u}_1+b\vec{u}_2au1​+bu2​ to a(10)+b(11)a\spmat{1\\0}+b\spmat{1\\1}a(10​)+b(11​). But of course, (10)\spmat{1\\0}(10​) is the representation of u1\vec{u}_1u1​ in the standard basis and (11)\spmat{1\\1}(11​) is the representation of u2\vec{u}_2u2​ in the standard basis, so these two vectors are actually the same object, just represented in terms of different bases. Here, we started with a vector expressed in BoldB_{old}Bold​ and ended up with the same vector expressed in the standard basis.

I spent a long time trying to reconcile these two interpretations. I wanted an explicit connection that showed that changing the basis like in the second interpretation was somehow the same action as the linear transformation. But you can’t really get around the fact that the vectors move in one interpretation and don’t move in the other. The reality is that the abstract nature of calculations like these open themselves to different interpretations which aren’t always strongly connected. Still though, I wanted a stronger intuition, instead of just being two ways of viewing the same calculation.

The One Dimensional Case: Imagine you have 3 meters of thread, and you want to know how many centimeters of thread you have. You might say that since there are 100cm in a meter, we would calculate:

(100cm/m)(3m)=300cm(100\textrm{cm/m})(3\textrm{m}) = 300\textrm{cm}(100cm/m)(3m)=300cm

Here we view 300cm and 3m as the same quantity, we’re just converting units. This is analogous to the “change of basis” interpretation. Alternatively, you might be a psycopath and say that since there are 100cm in a meter, then we simply need to transform every centimeter into 100cm by scaling by 100. Accordingly, 3cm is scaled as follows:

100(3cm)=3(100⋅1cm)=3(100cm)=300cm100(3\textrm{cm}) = 3(100\cdot 1\textrm{cm}) = 3(100\textrm{cm}) = 300\textrm{cm}100(3cm)=3(100⋅1cm)=3(100cm)=300cm

Here our world is measured in terms of 1cm, and then to get our answer we change the entire measurement system from counting in units of 1cm to units of 100cm. We don’t start with 3 meters and convert that into centimeters. Instead, that’s kind of baked into this new measurement system that counts in units of 100cm. This is analogous to the linear transformation interpretation. Of course, the two calculations are just multiplying 3 by 100.

The difference here is pretty subtle, and it was quite hard for me to understand where exactly the linear transformation approach differed from just how I typically think about unit conversion. But it then dawned on me that this was exactly what I was looking for: a strong intuition that connected the two distinctly different approaches. With this, the first question is answered.

Answer to Question 2: The columns of the change-of-basis matrix BBB do follow the same pattern, but it just doesn’t look like it since we originally expressed the vectors in terms of the standard basis. Taking the matrix CCC from the simplified problem, the iiith column is ui\vec{u}_iui​ relative to the standard basis (old basis in this case). Therefore, the iiith column of the matrix BBB should be vi\vec{v}_ivi​ relative to BoldB_{old}Bold​. Its easy to verify that this is the case:

−2u1+1u2=−2(10)+1(11)=(−11)=v1−1u1+1u2=−1(10)+1(11)=(01)=v2\begin{aligned} -2\vec{u}_1+1\vec{u}_2 &= -2\pmat{1\\0} + 1\pmat{1\\1} \\ &= \pmat{-1\\1} = \vec{v}_1 \\ -1\vec{u}_1+1\vec{u}_2 &= -1\pmat{1\\0}+1\pmat{1\\1} \\ &= \pmat{0\\1} = \vec{v}_2 \end{aligned}−2u1​+1u2​−1u1​+1u2​​=−2(10​)+1(11​)=(−11​)=v1​=−1(10​)+1(11​)=(01​)=v2​​

Thus, relative to BoldB_{old}Bold​, v1=(−21)\vec{v}_1 = \spmat{-2\\1}v1​=(−21​) and v2=(−11)\vec{v}_2 = \spmat{-1\\1}v2​=(−11​) as desired. Hence Question 2 has been answered.

4. Maybe the Real Change-of-Basis Matrix was the Friends We Made Along the Way

So where did all that leave me? What I now knew was that:

  1. The proper change-of-basis matrix was the inverse of what I had initially thought it should be.
  2. This inverted matrix makes sense because of how it acts on the basis vectors when thought of as a linear transformation.
  3. This linear transformation interpretation is strongly connected to the change of basis interpretation; they are two different ways to achieve the same result of “unit conversion”.
  4. I can calculate the change-of-basis matrix easily by first calculating what the new basis vectors are relative to the old basis. Then the columns of the change-of-basis matrix are just these resulting coordinate vectors.

But this didn’t tell me why my original matrix wasn’t the right one. After all, that matrix did take vectors expressed in the old basis to their coordinates relative to the new basis. How annoying!

Just kidding, I didn’t really care about that at all, since that’s just something that happens a lot. The two matrices are inverses, so it doesn’t really matter which one you pick to be the change-of-basis matrix. You can do everything you can do with one matrix with the other. You’d just have to flip some stuff around to make it equivalent. My guess is that the action on the basis vectors themselves seemed more straightforward, so that’s why that one was chosen for the definition. Unfortunately, that makes some things inconvenient, like the aforementioned relation wold=Bwnew\vec{w}_{old} = B\vec{w}_{new}wold​=Bwnew​. Wikipedia even comments that this is confusing, but with what I’ve covered in this post, I definitely feel a lot better about it, so I’m fine with that. You can’t win ‘em all, I guess.
